speaker: Doctor
text: Hello, I am Dr. Agent. I see you are a newborn presenting with feeding intolerance and bilious vomiting; these are urgent signs that often indicate a blockage in the intestines. To determine the exact cause, can you tell me exactly how long the baby has been vomiting and if there is any blood or "currant jelly" in the stool? Also, has the baby passed any meconium since birth?

speaker: Patient
text: Newborn, 3050-g (6-lb 12-oz) male, six hours post delivery. The newborn has had several episodes of bilious vomiting and is intolerant to feeding since birth. Was born at term following an uncomplicated pregnancy, though the mother missed several prenatal checkups. The patient's older brother underwent surgery for pyloric stenosis as an infant.

speaker: Doctor
text:
DIAGNOSIS READY: Intestinal Atresia (specifically jejunal or ileal atresia).

The combination of bilious vomiting and feeding intolerance starting immediately after birth, in the absence of meconium passage despite being six hours old, strongly suggests a distal intestinal obstruction such as intestinal atresia rather than pyloric stenosis (which typically presents later and with non-bilious vomiting) or malrotation with volvulus (which usually presents after the first few days of life). The family history of pyloric stenosis is a distractor; the clinical picture of a newborn who has not passed meconium and is vomiting bilious fluid is an emergency requiring surgical intervention.
